newsitem.title: USA: Stocks due for a breather, but that's been said before.
newsitem.headline: Stocks due for a breather, but that's been said before.

text.p: Two weeks and 300 Dow points into its election celebration, Wall Street is expected to pause for a much-needed rest this week after a string of eight straight record closing highs.

The surge, which began on Election Day and whose fury has at times left market watchers puzzled, is finally showing some signs of wear, said analysts, several of whom are openly yearning for a respite.
"This market has a long way to go on the upside in the long-term," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "But for the near-term we're in a danger zone."

The Dow Jones industrial average rose 35.03 points to close at 6,348.03 on Friday, posting a 128.21 point rise for the week. Over the last two weeks, including a 19.8 point gain in the session before Election Day, the Dow has risen a whopping 326.13 points, or 5.4 percent.

Over each of the last eight of those sessions, the Dow has closed at a record high, a streak that sent Wall Street historians scurrying to find the last occasion on which blue chips managed such a run.

"The trend followers are in command of this market for the time being and those of us who have been fighting the tape have been wrong," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.
In the process, the rally left sceptics burned again -- but not badly enough to change their minds.
Despite the stubborn nature of the run-up, which has resisted repeated predictions of a pause, those sceptics remain convinced some backtracking is inevitable.
"Wall Street tends to go to extremes and over the last couple of days we have gotten a little ahead of ourselves," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
However, as Bleier noted, the strongest buying interest remained focused on blue-chip stocks, a symptom of the lock-step approach with which investors are approaching the market.
"The market is in its most classic herd mentality," he said. "All of the institutions are chasing the same 'nifty-fifty' style names."

Most visible among those buyers remain mutual fund managers, such as at Fidelity's flagship Magellan Fund, which reported last week that it boosted equities by 5 percent to 88.9 percent of overall assets as of the end of September.
For fund managers, who have enough work finding ways to allocate the new cash that continues to flow to accounts, finding a home for any new cash raised by selling positions only adds to the burden.
"The problem is if you sell something you then have the problem of buying something else that is equally overpriced," Metz said.
Another problem is the investor-friendly economic environment of moderate growth without inflation, which makes it tough to justify selling.
"With long bonds yielding less than 6.5 percent and cash at under 5 percent, there's really no alternative," said Edgar Peters, chief investment strategist at PanAgora Asset Management Inc.
"As long as interest rates stay low, the market can continue rising because there's no reason for people to sell stocks," he said.
Upcoming economic data are unlikely to change that, as the week's calendar does not include any Wall Street focal points.
Tuesday will bring weekly retail sales figures and October housing starts, which are expected to edge higher to an annualized 1.44 million units.
Other data include international trade balance figures, due Wednesday, and weekly jobless claims, due Thursday. Economists expect new claims to rise by 4,000 to 332,000.

For the week, the Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks added 6.79 points to end at a record 737.62; the Nasdaq composite index rose 4.3 to 1,261.80; the American Stock Exchange index gained 5.02 to 585.41, and the NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks was up 3.7 at a new high of 390.02.
